If Leon didn't come back, they were down two people and their only light source. The water lapped softly at the edge of the hole. The basement was unrecognizable. Leon’s hands found the pipe just beneath the surface and clung to it hard. He didn’t kick — didn’t fight the current — just pulled himself forward along the ceiling, trying to save energy while he searched. The basement was wrong. The entire area was foreign — somehow both too small and too large at once — swollen and warped out of shape in unnatural, unrecognizable configurations. But the pressure folded in all the same. Columns were shattered. Furniture drifted like corpses. Concrete sheared open. Rebar jutted like bones from a ribcage halfway through collapse. The flashlight cut maybe four feet in any direction before the water swallowed it. Everything beyond that was shadow. The shadows kept looking like people. He grabbed at one — fabric, he'd thought, or an arm, or something — and his knuckles came back scraped against broken concrete. He grabbed at another and found a shelf corner. He stopped grabbing at shadows. Something had settled down here. That was the feeling of it — not abandoned, not empty, but claimed. The debris wasn't random the way one might expect from a flood. It had the quality of accumulation, of things drawn in and kept. The current moved through it in slow deliberate patterns that didn't quite match the angles of the space. He pushed deeper, ears roaring, light darting in frantic sweeps. Come on, Jake. Where are you? The dark lake water surfaced briefly at the back of his mind. The pressure of something large moving beneath— He pulled himself forward along the next pipe. Found the next one. Kept moving. He hauled forward one grip at a time, flashlight clamped in his fist, beam darting through the water like a scalpel. The current tugged hard now. Not enough to sweep him outright, but enough to throw him off course with every pull. He gritted his teeth, adjusted, and kept going. Shapes moved below him. Pale smears and dark shadows. He kicked once to steer around a floating chair and nearly slammed his shin into what might’ve been a filing cabinet. The pain lanced through his leg, and he winced tight against it, familiar panic sparking in the back of his throat. He forced it down. Focus. Focus. He swept the light again. Leon saw the movement first — a disturbance in the water below him, too deliberate for current, too rhythmic for debris — and angled the flashlight down. The Entity's claws had come through the floor. Not violently. Not dramatically. They'd simply grown there, pushing up through the concrete like roots push through a sidewalk — patient and inevitable and completely indifferent to what the floor thought about it. Three of them visible in the beam, dark and articulated and wrong in the specific way that things with too many joints were wrong. One of them had Jake. Not aggressively. That was the thing that made it worse. The claw had hooked itself into the fabric of his pant leg and was tugging — gently, almost playfully, letting him rise up a bit before smoothly sinking him again. Jake flailed violently against it, twisting, eyes wide, limbs kicking at what he had assumed was floating trash. He had been fighting something he couldn't see, and now that the light had found him, the shift in him was immediate and total. The stressed tension of I’m caught on something became the flailing panic of I can see what has me and those were completely different animals. Leon kicked sharp off the wall. He dropped fast, grabbing Jake around the torso, one arm clamping across his ribs as the other jammed the flashlight into the crook of his elbow as Jake grabbed at his arm, trying to climb him to freedom. He kicked down hard past Jake at the claw, connecting sharply along the edge. It flexed but held. Leon kicked again, striking where the claw curled. Jake screamed something underwater — more air bubbles than sound — as the tension tightened. The claw flinched sharply, ripping into the pant leg and almost tugging Jake out of Leon’s arms. He aimed another kick down, and another. The tip of the claw split, a shard slicing through Jake’s leg as the rest recoiled. The cut bloomed scarlet, the water drinking it fast. Jake thrashed, twisting hard against Leon's hold. The other claws lashed out immediately, reaching, trying to reclaim their prize. No time. Leon turned, twisting upward, dragging Jake through the chaos and out of range of the Entity’s claws. Jake was half-kicking, half-flailing, trying to help, but his strength was gone and his leg wouldn't move right. Leon could feel it — the dead weight setting in. His own limbs burned. His lungs were screaming. But the light still worked, and that beam led them cleanly up, sputtering bright against the ceiling until, at last, it found the edges of the gap. He never bothered looking back to see if the claws were following. In his mind, they were already reaching out for him from the dark. His fingers found the pipe again and dragged. He didn't look back. The hole was where he'd left it. They surfaced in a violent crash — Jake bursting first in a flailing panic, Leon a heartbeat behind, his shoulder cracking sharp against the tile. Chests heaving. Coughing. Gagging up water between breaths that tasted like blood and mold with enough force that if they had the breath for it, they would have surfaced screaming.
